msg.content:
<document>
<title>Wildlife of Antarctica</title>
<fragment>

Antarctica's cold deserts have some of the least diverse fauna in the world. Terrestrial vertebrates are limited to subantarctic islands, and even then they are limited in number.[12] Antarctica, including the subantarctic islands, has no natural fully terrestrial mammals, reptiles, or amphibians. Human activity has however led to the introduction in some areas of foreign species, such as rats, mice, chickens, rabbits, cats, pigs, sheep, cattle, reindeer, and various fish.[12] Invertebrates, such as beetle species, have also been introduced.[13]


</fragment>
<fragment>

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Regions | * Biogeographic realm
* Antarctic Peninsula
* East Antarctica
	+ ice sheet
	+ shield
* Extreme points
* Floristic Kingdom
* Islands
* South Pole
	+ South magnetic pole
* West Antarctica
	+ ice sheet
 |
| Bodies of Water | * Antarctic/Southern Ocean
* Lake CECs
* Lake Mercer
* Lake Vostok
* List of rivers
* McMurdo Sound
* Ross Sea
* Weddell Sea
 |
| Life | * Flora
* Microorganisms
* Wildlife
	+ Birds
	+ Mammals
	+ Krill
 |


</fragment>
<fragment>

The four species that inhabit sea ice are thought to make up 50% of the total biomass of the world's seals.[28] Crabeater seals have a population of around 15 million, making them one of the most numerous large animals on the planet.[29] The New Zealand sea lion (*Phocarctos hookeri*), one of the rarest and most localised pinnipeds, breeds almost exclusively on the subantarctic Auckland Islands, although historically it had a wider range.[30] Out of all permanent mammalian residents, the Weddell seals live the furthest south.[31]


There are 10 cetacean species found in the Southern Ocean; six baleen whales, and four toothed whales. The largest of these, the blue whale (*Balaenoptera musculus*), grows to 24 metres (79 ft) long weighing 84 tonnes. Many of these species are migratory, and travel to tropical waters during the Antarctic winter.[32] Orcas, which do not migrate, nonetheless regularly travel to warmer waters, possibly to relieve the stress the temperature has on their skin.[33]




</fragment>
<fragment>
### Land invertebrates

[edit]

![](image)A pair of *Belgica antarctica*, the only insect on mainland Antarctica.
Most terrestrial invertebrates are restricted to the subantarctic islands. Although there are very few species, those that do inhabit Antarctica have high population densities. In the more extreme areas of the mainland, such as the cold deserts, food webs are sometimes restricted to three nematode species, only one of which is a predator.[12] Many invertebrates on the subantarctic islands can live in subzero temperatures without freezing, whereas those on the mainland can survive being frozen.[13]


Mites and springtails make up most terrestrial arthropod species, although various spiders, beetles, and flies can be found.[12] Several thousand individuals from various mite and springtail species can be found in 1 square metre (10.8 sq ft). Beetles and flies are the most species rich insect groups on the islands. Insects play an important role in recycling dead plant material.[13]


</fragment>
<fragment>
See also: Antarctic realm and Climate of Antarctica

![](image)Elevation of the Antarctic terrain
Around 98% of continental Antarctica is covered in ice up to 4.7 kilometres (2.9 mi) thick.[1] Antarctica's icy deserts have extremely low temperatures, high solar radiation, and extreme dryness.[2] Any precipitation that does fall usually falls as snow, and is restricted to a band around 300 kilometres (186 mi) from the coast. Some areas receive as little as 50 mm (2.0 in) of precipitation annually. The coldest temperature recorded on Earth was −89.4 °C (−128.9 °F) at Vostok Station on the Antarctic Plateau.[1] Organisms that survive in Antarctica are often extremophiles.[2]


</fragment>
</document>

| Arctic desert |

The **Arctic desert** ecoregion (WWF ID: PA1101) is a terrestrial ecoregion that covers the island groups of Svalbard, Franz Josef Land, Severny Island and Severnaya Zemlya in the Arctic Ocean, above 75 degrees north latitude. The region is covered with glaciers, snow, and bare rock in a harshly cold environment. The temperature does rise above freezing for short periods in the summer, so some ice melt occurs, and the area supports colonies of sea birds and mammals.[1] It has an area of 161,400 square kilometres (62,300 sq mi).[2][3][4]




## Location and description

[edit]

The ecoregion stretches 2,000 km west-to-east, and 1,000 km north-to-south, across the Arctic Ocean north of Norway and Russia. It covers the island groups of Svalbard (Norway), Franz Josef Land (Russia), Severny Island (Russia), and Severnaya Zemlya (Russia).



## Climate

[edit]

The region has a Tundra (Koppen classification ET). This climate is characterized by long, cold winters and very short summers with at least one month averaging over 0 °C (32 °F) so that snow or ice might melt, but no month averages over 10 °C (50 °F). Mean precipitation at the Ernst Krenkel Observatory in Franz Josef Land has, since 1961, averaged 294 mm/year, with mean temperatures of −25.6 °C (−14.1 °F) in January, and 0.8 °C (33.4 °F) in July.[5]



## Flora and fauna

[edit]

Plant life is scarce due to the cold climate, but there is moss and lichen vegetation on 5-10% of the territory at low elevations and where bare rock or soil exists. The largest colonies of Ivory gull are found in the region, as well as Atlantic walrus and Polar bear.



## Protections

[edit]

Over 36% of the ecoregion is in an officially protected area,[4] including all or a portion of:



* Forlandet National Park (Norway), covering Prins Karls Forland (island).
* Nordaust-Svalbard Nature Reserve (Norway), covering many islands in the Svalbard archipelago, much of which is glaciated,
* Nordvest-Spitsbergen National Park (Norway), covering the northwestern portion of Spitsbergen island.
* Nordre Isfjorden National Park (Norway), covering a fjord in central Spitzbergen
* Russian Arctic National Park (Russia), covering Franz Josef Land, the northern tip of Severnaya Zemly, and other islands.
* Sør-Spitsbergen National Park (Norway), covering the southern portion of Spitsbergen island.
* Søraust-Svalbard Nature Reserve (Norway), covering the southeastern portion of the Svalbard archipelago.


## See also

[edit]

* List of ecoregions in Russia
* List of ecoregions in Europe

We might not need exact article, we can use general knowledge. Provide answer summarizing four largest deserts and dominant animal types.

Thus answer:

1. Antarctic Desert – polar desert; dominant animal life: marine mammals (seals, whales) and seabirds (penguins, skuas); on land dominated by microorganisms, nematodes, mites, springtails.

2. Arctic Desert – polar desert; dominant animal life: marine mammals (walrus, polar bears) and seabirds (Ivory gull); also Arctic fox, lemmings.

3. Sahara Desert – hot sub‑tropical desert; dominant animal life: reptiles (lizards, snakes) and arthropods (scorpions, beetles); also small mammals (gerbils) and birds.

4. Great Australian Desert – arid continental desert; dominant animal life: marsupials (kangaroo rats? actually marsupial mammals like the bilby, marsupial mouse, kangaroo, banded hare-wallaby) and reptiles (bearded dragons, goannas); plus insects.

Will answer with concise table.

content:
**The four biggest deserts on Earth (by total area) and the type of animal life that dominates each**

| Rank | Desert (area) | Climate / “type” | Dominant animal group (what you’ll find most of) | Typical examples |
|------|----------------|------------------|---------------------------------------------------|------------------|
| **1** | **Antarctic Desert** – ~14 million km² | Polar (ice‑covered, extremely dry) | **Marine‑derived fauna & extremophile terrestrial invertebrates** – the land surface itself supports almost no vertebrates; life is dominated by seabirds, seals, whales and a huge abundance of microscopic/soil invertebrates (nematodes, mites, springtails). | Emperor & Adélie penguins, Weddell & crabeater seals, orca, blue whale; *Belgica antarctica* (the only Antarctic insect), springtails, nematodes. |
| **2** | **Arctic Desert** – ~13.9 million km² | Polar (tundra, ice‑covered islands) | **Marine mammals & seabirds** – the few ice‑free patches host large colonies of birds and the surrounding sea ice supports the region’s biggest predators. | Polar bear, Atlantic walrus, ivory gull, snow bunting, Arctic fox (on the few vegetated spots). |
| **3** | **Sahara Desert** – ~9.2 million km² | Hot‑subtropical (sand dunes, gravel plains) | **Reptiles and arthropods** – because of the extreme heat and scarcity of water, cold‑blooded vertebrates and insects are far more numerous than mammals. | Horned viper, sand lizard, desert monitor, Saharan silver ant, scorpions, beetles; small mammals (gerbils, jerboas) are present but far less abundant. |
| **4** | **Great Australian Desert** – ~2.7 million km² (the combined “Great Australian Desert” – a mosaic of the Simpson, Great Victoria, Great Sandy & other arid zones) | Arid‑subtropical (spinifex grasslands, sand plains) | **Marsupials and reptiles** – Australian arid lands are dominated by native marsupial mammals plus a rich reptile fauna; insects are also abundant but vertebrate biomass is largely marsupial‑reptile. | Bilby, spinifex hopping mouse, marsupial mole, red kangaroo, bearded dragon, goanna, thorny devil; numerous beetles and termites. |

### Why these groups dominate

| Desert | Reason the listed group dominates |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| **Antarctic** | The continent is ice‑covered; only a thin coastal fringe receives enough sunlight for any terrestrial life. The food web is driven by the surrounding Southern Ocean, so marine mammals and seabirds (which feed at sea) are the bulk of the vertebrate biomass. On land, only extremophiles (nematodes, mites, springtails) can survive the cold, dryness and lack of vegetation. |
| **Arctic** | Similar to Antarctica, most of the area is sea‑ice. The richest animal communities are the sea‑ice‑dependent mammals (walrus, polar bear) and the large seabird colonies (e.g., ivory gull). Terrestrial mammals are few and limited to ice‑free coastal zones. |
| **Sahara** | Temperatures often exceed 45 °C and water is scarce. Ectothermic reptiles can regulate body temperature behaviorally and need far less water than mammals, so they out‑number vertebrate mammals. Arthropods (especially ants, beetles, scorpions) thrive in the sand and have rapid life cycles that cope with the harsh climate. |
| **Great Australian Desert** | Australia’s long isolation produced a suite of marsupials uniquely adapted to aridity (e.g., bilby, hopping mouse). Reptiles are also highly successful in the hot, dry environment. The sparse vegetation (spinifex) supports these herbivores and their predators, while insects dominate the detrital layer. |

**Take‑away:**  
- The two polar deserts are dominated by **marine‑linked fauna** (seals, whales, seabirds) plus microscopic terrestrial invertebrates.  
- The hot non‑polar deserts are dominated by **cold‑blooded vertebrates and arthropods** (reptiles, insects) because they can survive the extreme heat and water scarcity.  
- Australia’s huge arid zone is a **marsupial‑reptile** world, reflecting the continent’s unique evolutionary history.
